01 · Product I built · Solo

TallyRAX — making expense tracking survive a normal week

A conversational money-logging app built on one bet: that recording a transaction can feel closer to writing a thought than filling out an accounting form.

RoleProduct owner & builder (solo)
TimelineMay – July 2026
StagePrivate beta, collecting feedback
PlatformAndroid · React Native · Supabase

Typing “Movie tickets 800” → auto-categorized as Entertainment and saved instantly, transaction count ticking up, with one-tap Undo. No form. No confirm step.

Decision 01
Focused on one customer before expanding.
Narrowed from three personas to one independent professional to eliminate conflicting requirements and build a more coherent MVP.
Decision 02
Kept natural-language input. Removed the chatbot interface.
Preserved the speed of conversational logging while avoiding a chat experience that distracted from the core task.
Decision 03
Chose deterministic categorization over AI.
The rule-based parser correctly categorized 96% of common transactions in internal testing. For an MVP handling financial data, reliability mattered more than broader language understanding.
Decision 04
Optimized for fast correction over perfect prediction.
Rather than trying to understand every possible input, the product made corrections quick and used them to improve future parsing rules.

The problem

People don't lack finance tools. They lack one that survives a normal week. Bank apps show what already happened, weeks late. Spreadsheets demand upkeep no one sustains. Expense trackers front-load the cost — pick a category, choose an account, tag it, confirm — for every ₹40 chai. They ask for accounting behavior from someone who never signed up to be an accountant. The failure isn't motivation; it's that every entry is taxed until the user quietly stops. And once logging stops, every downstream feature sits on data that doesn't exist.

Honest note on evidence: this framing is reasoned from public discussions and the problem itself, not formal user research. The personas below are decision tools, not validated segments.

The first real decision was cutting a user

"People who struggle with their finances" describes everyone and specifies no one. Three provisional personas — a freelancer, a small-business owner, a shop owner — looked like one problem but weren't. A feature set powerful enough for the business owner would overwhelm the shop owner; every new user type quietly expanded the product until TallyRAX was becoming a smaller version of the tools it meant to replace. So the first move wasn't adding a feature. It was cutting the business owner as a user — and the problem statement moved with her, from "people need better bookkeeping" to "people need a lower-effort way to stay aware."

Why it didn't become a chatbot

The earliest model was a conversational assistant. On paper, the lowest-friction version. Mapping the full flow broke it: chat is optimized for conversation, but financial records are optimized for correction, scanning, and trust — none of which a chat log does well. A single wrong transaction buried in a thread raised questions the model couldn't answer cleanly. Natural-language input survived; the conversation interface didn't.

Building intelligence without making AI the product

A creative answer is useful in conversation and dangerous when categorizing someone's money. So instead of sending every transaction to a model, TallyRAX runs a local, rule-based pipeline first — and only leans on automation where confidence is high.

Input → "Swiggy 240"
Direction detection → Expense
Merchant recognition → Swiggy detected
Category mapping → Food
Transaction created → saved instantly
User corrects → Food → Subscription · and it sticks next time

Ambiguity is handled by correction, not prediction. "Coursera 799" might be education for one person and a subscription for another. Rather than guess perfectly, the app saves immediately, makes the fix lightweight — and each correction becomes a future rule. The product gets more personal through use, not more complicated up front.

The failure that was worth having

The first external beta appeared to work: transactions logged, and the app felt functional. The real problem surfaced only later — a release configuration error had stopped production data from reaching the backend. The app had been validated; the release itself hadn't.

The lesson wasn't technical. A working feature is only valuable if it produces trustworthy user feedback. Every release afterward followed one checklist: deploy, verify production data, then recruit testers. Shipping code and shipping a product are not the same thing.

Where it stands — and what I'd measure

No usage results to claim yet, and I won't manufacture them. The current cohort is me and two others — not a sample anyone should draw conclusions from. But the app is instrumented (Sentry for reliability, PostHog for behavior), so each bet becomes a real number the moment there's a cohort worth measuring:

  • Logging survives — are testers still logging in weeks 2–3 without prompts? The North Star.
  • The parser earns trust — correction rate after save. Low = trustworthy; high = automation is failing.
  • Capture beats forms — time-to-first-saved-transaction from app open. The direct test of the premise.
  • Insights are worth the interruption — engagement vs. dismissal on surfaced patterns.
Build MVP
↓ Prepare external beta
↓ Release blocked by Supabase configuration bug
↓ Bug fixed
↓ Private beta restarted
↓ Currently collecting early user feedback

What I'd do next

Next experiment: get TallyRAX in front of 15–30 people who aren't friends or family — recruited from the same communities where I found the problem — so the bets above become real numbers instead of intuitions.

Biggest unknown: whether conversational logging survives past the novelty of week one. Everything else is downstream of that.

Still unvalidated: that fast correction actually rebuilds trust after a wrong guess. The flow is designed for it, but I haven't watched enough real users hit a mistake to know whether it holds.

The biggest lesson so far: building something useful was less about adding intelligence and more about removing everything that made users need it. The product got smaller and the problem got clearer — defined tightly enough that the next beta can finally prove the bet right or wrong. That's the progress: not a finished answer, but a question sharp enough to be worth testing.

02 · Product teardown · AI PM exercise

Google AI Overview: the trust gap nobody is measuring

When an answer engine inherits the interface of a search engine, the contract with the user changes — but the interface never evolved to signal it. This teardown is about that gap.

LensAI product judgment · Strategy
MethodMulti-week testing + Ahrefs, Pew, Semrush, Similarweb data
FormatFull teardown · 13-min read

AI Overview isn't asking whether it's accurate enough — everyone asks that. The real question is whether the product design earned the trust it's requesting. Top placement, confident prose, and no uncertainty signals give it the authority of neutral search without the neutrality that once justified it.

It starts with the constraint, not the critique

~$237B of Alphabet's revenue depends on users clicking links. An answer engine that completes the task without a click is in structural conflict with the model that funds it. Every design choice — what AI Overview triggers on, what it signals, what happens when it's wrong — happens inside that constraint. Naming it first is what separates a critique from a PM recommendation.

The core failure: felt trust vs. earned trust

Citations look like they solve the trust problem. They don't — roughly 1% of users click them. They create the appearance of verification without the function, outsourcing the work to users who behaviorally aren't doing it. Google already proves it can signal uncertainty (health queries get disclaimers and confidence indicators); it applies that capability only where regulatory pressure is visible. I watched AI Overview invent a framework that doesn't exist from a garbled voice query, cite nine sources, and present it with the same authority as a fact.

The measurement trap

Google's stated success signal — did users engage with the Overview — cannot distinguish a satisfied user from one who read it, found it insufficient, and scrolled past. A trigger system optimized on that signal will never self-correct for its biggest misfire: exploration-seeking queries that need breadth, not a single synthesized answer.

Three fixes — each naming what it costs

  • Split informational intent into explanation- vs. exploration-seeking; suppress AI Overview on the latter. Cost: less AI surface area at the moment Google needs users to see it as ChatGPT-competitive.
  • Add real uncertainty signals to general queries, measured by citation-click lift. Cost: visible uncertainty may reduce perceived authority — the central tension.
  • Rebuild the success metric around task completion per intent sub-type. Cost: better instrumentation may surface inconvenient data that slows expansion.

AI Overview isn't a bad product — it's one in a genuinely hard position. Most of the decisions have a plausible internal justification. That's the point: the choices weren't irrational, they just added up to an interface that signals more trust than the system has earned. That gap is what an AI PM should be measuring.

What I'd want to validate

My core claim — that visible uncertainty signals would raise verification without gutting usefulness — is a hypothesis, not a finding. The first thing I'd run is the citation-click test: add a recency timestamp or source-consensus indicator to a slice of general queries and watch whether citation click-through moves off its 1% floor. If it doesn't, my read of the trust gap is wrong, and I'd want to learn that early.

03 · A PRD for Agentic Coding Tools

Designing AI That Knows When to Ask

Agentic coding tools treat the line between "ask" and "proceed" as a property of the action. This spec argues it is also a property of the user — and the user moves. A checkpoint policy that produces genuine oversight in week one produces the appearance of oversight by week twelve.

FormatSelf-directed PRD — a design proposal, not a shipped feature
LensProduct decisions under uncertainty · trade-off analysis
Grounded inClaude Code Auto Mode · mixed-initiative & AI-confidence research · a public user thread

Action classifiers ask whether this action is risky. The mixed-initiative literature asks who should hold initiative for this task. Neither asks whether the person receiving the escalation is still reading it. This spec sits on top of action-classification and addresses only that gap — it does not try to rebuild the classifier.

The problem: oversight decays, and no design tells decay apart from maturation

Vendor usage data shows auto-approve rates rising from roughly 20% to over 40% as users gain experience, humans making about 70% of planning decisions but only 20% of execution decisions, and a single prompt triggering around 10 agent actions on average — some stretches running past 100 actions between human touchpoints. The honest complication: the source frames this as maturation, not a problem. Both readings fit the same data, and no current design distinguishes them.

A small public signal that users feel the difference: in one r/ArtificialIntelligence thread, one user wanted to stay in the driver's seat and catch mistakes before they spiral; another replied that this already exists, citing an interruptible agent; the first answered that a comparable tool moved too fast for them to catch anything. Two users, the same feature set, opposite verdicts — a disagreement about calibration, not capability, which is exactly what a static classifier cannot supply.

The failure this produces: a user who approves reflexively is not supervised — yet the system, the audit log, and the user all record the interaction as supervision. That is worse than no checkpoint, because it manufactures a record of oversight that never happened.

Four product decisions — each named with the trade-off it accepts

Decision 01
The approval threshold is a function of user state, not action class alone.
The classifier decides what could warrant a stop; this layer decides whether a stop will actually be read. Trade-off: it now models the user — inference people resent when it's wrong and don't notice when it's right, justified only by the tail.
Decision 02
Detect decay from approval latency, not approval rate.
A high approval rate fits both a good classifier and a user who stopped reading; latency disambiguates. Trade-off: latency is noisy — and whether it correlates with review at all is the spec's load-bearing, untested assumption.
Decision 03
Respond to decay by re-earning attention, not adding checkpoints.
More stops for an inattentive user accelerate the decay; instead the next high-consequence stop gets heavier — the diff, the specific ambiguity, a substantive input. Trade-off: fewer, heavier interruptions concentrate risk on picking the right stop.
Decision 04
Express confidence behaviorally, never numerically.
Low confidence narrows scope and asks, rather than showing a percentage; research shows miscalibrated numeric confidence degrades reliance and users can't detect it. Trade-off: users who want to set a numeric threshold can't.

How it would be judged

North-star metric: reverted agent commits — a direct proxy for errors that escaped review. Guardrail: the approval-latency distribution over tenure, which is the decay curve this layer exists to flatten. Counter-metric: time-to-completion, which rises if the layer over-fires. Diagnostic: the disable rate — users switching it off is the cleanest possible verdict. Latency and completion time have to be read together, since either alone can be moved by pushing the threshold one way.

The honest evaluation problem: the only direct test of whether someone is reviewing is an in-session probe that injects a detectable discrepancy and checks whether they catch it — which means deliberately showing users something wrong. That tension is real, I have not resolved it, and I would not ship the probe without a resolution.

What I'd validate first — and the limits of the evidence

The load-bearing open question is whether approval latency correlates with review at all; Decision 02 depends on it entirely and it is untested. The second is whether rising auto-approve rates are decay or earned trust — the design's value depends on which dominates, and the published data doesn't separate them (resolvable by correlating auto-approve rate against downstream revert rate).

Evidence limitations, stated plainly: the user signal is four public comments from a single thread — enough to establish that the tension exists, not to size it. The decay data is vendor-published, not independent measurement. No primary user research was conducted for this spec.

How I work Four habits that show up across the work — drawn from the projects, not from a framework.
01

Cut scope before adding it

The first real decision on TallyRAX wasn't a feature — it was removing a user. A product is easier to trust when it can point to what it deliberately leaves out.

02

Validate the behavior before the technology

Rule-based categorization shipped before any AI, because the open question was whether people would log conversationally at all — not how smart the model was.

03

Match recovery to the cost of the mistake

For low-stakes, reversible errors — a mis-categorized transaction in TallyRAX — fast, obvious correction beats chasing perfect accuracy. But recovery only helps when a mistake is reversible and the user notices it. For irreversible or invisible errors, the design job is prevention, not a good undo.

04

Separate what's proven from what's reasoned

Each claim is marked as evidence or inference. A decision that can be defended is worth more than a number that can't be stood behind.
